title: The stricter Roman sense of moral good: the natural law kept without rising above nature
source_text: IV. Hoc sensu bonum morale a Protestantibus frequenter usurpatur, ut praesertim videre est in thesibus Salmuriensibus. In hac vero disputatione Scholae Romanae Theologi bonum morale paulo strictius sumunt. Nam bonum morale opponunt non tantum bono naturae seu Physico, sed etiam bono supernaturali. Adeoque sub bono morali non comprehendunt virtutes Theologicas, sive infusas, & actus inde promanantes qui sunt ordinis supernaturalis; sed solum omne illud quod rectae rationi & legi naturae conforme est, & tamen supra naturam non assurgit. Ac proinde totum illud bonum positum est in observatione legis illius, quae naturaliter cordi hominis est inscripta, quam Deus in Decalogo summatim comprehendit, & quae non est aliud quam rectae rationis dictamen.
pass_a_gloss: IV. In this sense moral good is frequently used by the Protestants, as is especially to be seen in the Saumur theses. But in this disputation the Theologians of the Roman School take moral good a little more strictly. For they oppose moral good not only to the good of nature or Physical good, but also to supernatural good. And so under moral good they do not comprehend the Theological virtues, or infused ones, and the acts flowing thence which are of the supernatural order; but only all that which is conformed to right reason and the law of nature, and yet does not rise above nature. And accordingly that whole good is placed in the observance of that law which is naturally inscribed on the heart of man, which God summarily comprehended in the Decalogue, and which is nothing else than the dictate of right reason.
pass_b_english: Protestants often use 'moral good' in this sense, as can be seen above all in the Saumur theses. In this dispute, however, the theologians of the Roman School take it a little more strictly. They set moral good not only against the good of nature, or physical good, but also against supernatural good.

So they do not include under moral good the theological or infused virtues and the acts that flow from them, which belong to the supernatural order. They include only what agrees with right reason and the law of nature without rising above nature. On their view the whole of that good consists in keeping the law written by nature on the human heart, which God summed up in the Decalogue and which is nothing other than the dictate of right reason.

lemmas.latin: quae naturaliter cordi hominis est inscripta
lemmas.gloss: which is naturally inscribed on the heart of man

choices.why: The Schools' term for the good that earns praise or reward and makes a man good without qualification; kept as 'moral good', with the narrower Roman sense explained in the text.
